title: "First half – The claim and its reproduction"
---
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Slides.** [Open the deck at this half](../../slides/housing-short.html#/half-1-the-claim-and-its-reproduction){target="_blank"} in its own tab, or follow it on the [slides page](slides.qmd).
:::

The first half gives you the vocabulary of three kinds of repetition and the case, an experiment run by email, and works out what question its claim answers. Before the break you reproduce the result that one of the five independent analysts of the claim reported, and find out why your number is exactly that number.

| Work through | What you do | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Slides, the opening | The plan of the session, and what you do not need: no git, and no GitHub or OSF account. | 3 minutes |
| Slides, the first half | The matrix of data against analysis that separates reproducibility, robustness and replicability; the SCORE programme in brief; and Multi100 from the inside: what an analyst received, the two tasks, and how the results were put on a common scale. | 12 minutes |
| Your workspace, or [Browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-1-setup) Task 1 | Task 1, the setup check. Confirm that `source("R/check_setup.R")` prints OK on every line, the last check reporting −19.97 percentage points, or that the browser lab has loaded `audit` with 1,014 rows. If your machine will not cooperate, carry on in the browser lab. | 5 minutes |
| Slides, the paper and the five analysts | The paper of the original authors (OAs): the question that it asks, the design, the email word for word, what came back for each of the six names, the four outcomes that were coded, and the claim as SCORE selected it. Then the five Multi100 analysts, with five different questions behind two different verdicts. | 18 minutes |
| Slides, the estimand and the graph | The estimand statement, which everyone writes in chat, holds and sends together; the causal graph of the experiment; why comparing greetings among the replies conditions on a consequence of the name; and what changes when every delivered email is counted. | 12 minutes |
| Slides, the reproduction | The instruction of Task 2 of Multi100 read word for word, what it left open, and the aim of the reproduction: the chi-square test that analyst 8PTRZ ran on the public file of the OAs. | 6 minutes |
| Task 3 in your report or working script, or [Browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-3-reproduction) Task 3 | Read the public file `audit_original.csv`, keep the replies that carry a greeting code, mark the Hispanic names, build the two-by-two table and pass it to `chisq.test()`. It should give $\chi^2$ = 14.265 on 558 replies, the value that Multi100 recorded for 8PTRZ. Everyone types their value without sending it and sends it when the facilitator says go. | 14 minutes |
| Slides | The continuity correction, which `chisq.test()` applies to a two-by-two table unless it is told otherwise, so that `correct = FALSE` gives 14.95; and why the whole class got the same value while the five analysts, each writing their own code, did not. | 5 minutes |

**By the end of the half** you have written the estimand statement behind the claim, you know why comparing among the replies and counting every delivered email answer two different questions, and you have reproduced $\chi^2$ = 14.265 yourself and know why it is not 14.95.
